performers.title: 🚀 Water on Mars: The Vanishing Act
performers.hook: Pour water on Mars and it vanishes
performers.script: Pour water on Mars and it vanishes. Thin atmosphere, low pressure. Water boils instantly, then freezes. On Venus, it's crushed by pressure. On Jupiter, it's lost in gas. But what happens to water on other planets? Pour water on Mars and it vanishes

performers.title: UNSOLVED #46 | 🚨 Green Skies Before Tornadoes: Nature’s Unsolved Alarm 🌪️
performers.hook: The sky turning green isn’t magic—it’s a warning sign you can’t ignore!
performers.script: When a supercell loads massive hail, the cloud becomes a dense, water‑filled curtain that scatters sunlight, stripping away longer wavelengths and leaving an eerie green flash like a natural alarm. Meteorologists say the green hue warns of the fiercest tornadoes, but why it shows green instead of yellow or blue is still unknown. As the vortex draws near, the green glow swells, then vanishes in the roar—take cover instantly, watch the sky!
performers.topic: Why the sky turns green before a tornado

performers.title: HOW IT WORKS #32 | 💥 The Shrimp That Fires a Sun‑Hot Bubble!
performers.hook: A shrimp can fire a bubble that burns hotter than the surface of the sun.
performers.script: When the pistol shrimp snaps its claw, a rapid water jet creates a vapor cavity that collapses in microseconds, forming a shock wave that reaches 210 dB. The collapse super‑heats the gas to 5,000 °C, ionizing it and emitting a flash of blue light—a phenomenon called sonoluminescence. The shock knocks the prey unconscious, and the flash blinds them, leaving no chance to flee. In seconds, the shrimp's tiny claw becomes a weapon of sound and fire, turning a simple pond into a battlefield of invisible blasts.
performers.topic: The pistol shrimp's bubble‑shock and flash

performers.title: HOW IT WORKS #20 | 🔭 Gold Mirror Reveals the Universe’s First Light!
performers.hook: A 20‑kilogram gold mirror peers back 13 billion years.
performers.script: A 20‑kilogram gold mirror peers back 13 billion years. JWST’s 18 hexagonal segments are coated in a thin layer of gold, turning invisible infrared photons into bright reflections. The reflected light races through a chilled instrument suite to detectors that turn ancient heat signatures into images. Each photon carries the universe’s earliest glow, stretched by expansion into the infrared we can now capture. A crystal‑clear snapshot of the cosmos when it was only a few hundred million years old, the baby picture of everything we see today.
performers.topic: James Webb Telescope's gold-coated mirror and early galaxies
